descricao: Body parts from head to toe, action verbs, exercise vocabulary, and tricky plurals.

secoes.titulo: From Head to Toe: The Big Picture
secoes.conteudo:
Let's start with a quick question. If a doctor asks you 'Where does it hurt?' and you do not know the word in English, what do you do? Point and hope? That works sometimes — but not always. Knowing the names of your body parts is one of the most practical things you can learn in any language.

Let's do a tour from top to bottom. At the very top: your **head**. On your head, you have your **face** — and on your face, your **forehead** (the area above your eyes), your **cheeks** (the soft sides of your face), and your **chin** (the bottom part). Your **neck** connects your head to the rest of your body.

Moving down: you have two **shoulders** at the top of your body, connecting your **arms**. In the front, you have your **chest**. Behind, your **back**. Below your chest: your **stomach** (or **belly**, in informal English — same thing). Lower still: your **hips**, and then your two **legs**. At the bottom of each leg: your **foot**. Now here is one of the most important irregular plurals in English: one **foot**, two **feet**. Not 'foots' — **feet**. You will use this every day, so lock it in now.

Connecting your foot to your leg is your **ankle**. The front of your lower leg is your **shin**, and the back is your **calf**. In the middle of each leg: your **knee**. And the upper part of your leg — the big area between your hip and your knee — is your **thigh**. A very useful word when you are describing pain or injury.

Now let's go deeper. These are the smaller body parts that come up all the time — especially when something hurts, or when you are describing someone precisely.

Let's start with the **arm**. At the very end of your arm: your **hand**. Each hand has five **fingers**. The short, thick one on the side is specifically called your **thumb** — not a finger, specifically a **thumb**. At the tip of each finger: a **fingernail**. At the bottom of your arm, where it connects to your hand: your **wrist**. And in the middle of your arm, where it bends: your **elbow**. A lot of people forget **wrist** and **elbow** — they are the two arm joints. Remember them.

On your face: your two **eyes**, each framed by **eyelashes** — the thin hairs along the edges. On the sides of your head: your two **ears**. In the center of your face: your **nose**. And your **mouth**, which has **lips** on the outside and **teeth** on the inside. Now, tooth → **teeth** is the other essential irregular plural. One tooth, many **teeth**. Not 'tooths' — **teeth**. Tooth and teeth. Foot and feet. These two are the most important irregular plurals in the body vocabulary.

Your **shoulder** — the joint at the top of each arm — was mentioned already, but it deserves a second look. In Portuguese, the shoulder is 'ombro,' a single clear word. In English, **shoulder** works the same way: it is the round joint where your arm meets your upper body. If someone asks you to give them a massage, this is the area they probably want.

secoes.titulo: What Your Body Does: Action Verbs
secoes.conteudo:
Your body is not just a collection of parts — it does things. And many of those actions have specific verbs in English that are very useful to know.

Some verbs are tied to specific body parts. Your eyes **blink** automatically — you do not even think about it, your eyes just close and open very quickly every few seconds. You **smile** when you are happy, using your mouth and face. You **chew** food with your teeth before you swallow. You **smell** things with your nose. And you **see** with your eyes — but there is an important difference between **see** and **look** and **watch**. You **see** something without trying ('I saw a bird outside'). You **look** at something on purpose ('Look at this photo!'). You **watch** something that moves or changes over time ('I watched a film last night'). Three different verbs, all related to your eyes.

With your hands and arms: you **clap** when you are happy — you hit your two hands together repeatedly. You **wave** to say hello or goodbye from a distance. You **point** to show someone where something is, usually with your **index finger** (the one next to your thumb). You **touch** things to feel their texture. And you **write** — something so common we forget it is a physical action.

With your legs and feet: you **walk**, **run**, **jump**, and **kick**. These four verbs describe the most basic movements people make. **Walk** is the slow everyday movement. **Run** is faster. **Jump** is up into the air. **Kick** is using your foot to hit something — like a football.

If you follow fitness content, yoga videos, or go to the gym — or if you just want to understand what a personal trainer is telling you — this vocabulary is essential.

First, a useful distinction. **Aerobic exercise** is movement that gets your **heart** beating faster and makes you **breathe** harder. Running, cycling, swimming, and basketball are all aerobic. The word comes from Greek and means 'with air' — these exercises demand a lot of oxygen. Your **lungs** work harder to bring in more air, and your heart pumps that oxygen-rich blood to your whole body.

**Flexibility exercise** is different. Instead of speeding up your heart, it makes your body easier to move. Yoga, martial arts, and dance are examples. These exercises strengthen your **muscles** (the soft tissue that moves your bones) and your **bones** themselves, making it easier to move freely as you get older.

Now the action verbs for exercise. **Stretch** means to extend a muscle as far as it will comfortably go — you feel a pull, but not pain. **Bend** means to curve a part of your body — you bend your knees, you bend your arm. **Straighten** is the opposite — you make something straight again after bending. **Raise** means to lift something up — you raise your arm, you raise your leg. **Turn** means to rotate — you turn your head, you turn your body to the left.

A few more: **stand** means to be in a vertical position on your feet. **Breathe** means to take air in and let it out — simple, but in exercise, breathing technique makes a big difference. **Shake** means to move something quickly from side to side — you shake your arms to relax them. And **touch** in exercise often means bringing one body part to another: 'touch your toes' means bend forward until your fingers reach your feet.

secoes.titulo: Irregular Plurals and Things That Confuse Portuguese Speakers
secoes.conteudo:
Let's finish with a few things that often confuse Portuguese speakers specifically.

The two most important irregular plurals in body vocabulary: one **foot**, two **feet**. One **tooth**, many **teeth**. These do not follow the normal -s rule, and they come up constantly. Say them a few times out loud: foot, feet. Tooth, teeth. They should feel automatic.

A word on **muscle**. In Portuguese, 'músculo' is pronounced roughly as it is written. In English, **muscle** is pronounced 'MUS-ul' — the 'c' is completely silent, and the 'le' at the end is just an 'ul' sound. If you say 'MUS-cle' with the c, English speakers will understand you, but it will sound a little off. The silent c in **muscle** is one of those small things that makes a difference.

Now, **wrist** versus **ankle**. Both of these are joints — one on your arm, one on your leg. Portuguese speakers sometimes mix them up because both connect a limb to an extremity. Simple rule: **wrist** is on your arm (between hand and arm), **ankle** is on your leg (between foot and leg). Wrist = arm. Ankle = leg.

And one last word worth knowing: **elbow**. In Portuguese, 'cotovelo' is clear enough. In English, **elbow** sounds nothing like any Portuguese word, so it just needs to be memorized. You have two elbows — the joints in the middle of your arms where they bend. Next time you rest your chin on your hand while reading, notice your **elbow** on the table. Now you will always remember it.
